notes: Sidney Madwed was a real motivational speaker and poet whose lines circulate widely on aggregator sites, and this one is consistently attributed to him, but I cannot place it in any book, article, or speech transcript I know of. The claim itself ('the subconscious cannot tell the difference between reality and imagination') is a stock New Thought / self-help proposition that predates Madwed by decades, so he may be restating rather than originating it. No citation available.

The idea is genuinely Freud's: he described thinking as 'Probehandeln' — trial or experimental action — notably in 'Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning' (1911), where thought is characterized as experimental action carried out with small quantities of energy, and again in later work. 'Thought is action in rehearsal' is a compressed English aphorism of that concept rather than any translator's rendering I can point to in the Standard Edition. Attribution to Freud is sound at the level of idea; the exact wording is popularizer's phrasing, so I am holding this below the promotion bar.

earliest_print_source: The Hound of the Baskervilles, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1902
notes: Spoken by Sherlock Holmes in 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' (1902), early in the novel. The canonical wording is 'The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes' — the corpus text substitutes 'notices' for 'observes' and inserts a comma. Recommend restoring the published wording. Note also that this is a fictional character's line, not Conan Doyle speaking in his own voice.

earliest_print_source: Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton, David Brewster, 1855
notes: Newton's seashore remark is well documented, but the corpus text is a loose paraphrase, not the recorded wording. The standard version: 'I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' Recorded by Joseph Spence (Anecdotes, collected in Newton's lifetime, published 1820) and given wide currency by Brewster's 1855 Memoirs. 'Searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell' is a modern rewrite. High confidence Newton said something very close to this; low confidence in this specific text, hence attributed rather than verified. Strongly recommend replacing with the canonical wording.

Consistently attributed to Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury) across quotation collections, and it is stylistically at home in his popular essay collections 'The Pleasures of Life' (1887) and 'The Use of Life' (1894). I believe it comes from one of those two, but I cannot state which with confidence, so I am not citing a source. Lubbock is not a misattribution magnet and the attribution is stable, which supports a moderate rating; the missing citation keeps it below the bar.

earliest_print_source: "Do Schools Kill Creativity?", TED talk, Ken Robinson, February 2006
notes: A well-known line from Robinson's February 2006 TED talk 'Do Schools Kill Creativity?', in the passage arguing that children will take a chance and are not frightened of being wrong. The same argument appears in his book 'Out of Our Minds: Learning to Be Creative'. Wording in the talk is 'If you're not prepared to be wrong, you'll never come up with anything original' — matches the corpus text.

Churchill is a documented misattribution magnet and this line has no primary source I can identify in his speeches, books, or letters. It circulates in two forms: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth...' (the older form, found in mid-20th-century Churchill anecdote compilations) and the later gender-neutral 'Everyone stumbles...' variant used here. Churchill quotation scholarship treats sayings of this kind that surface only in compiled anecdote books with suspicion. Plausible but unconfirmed; the corpus text is in any case the later rewritten variant, not the earliest attributed form.

The Churchill attribution is spurious. This is a modern variant of a saying with a long documented pedigree: Jonathan Swift wrote 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it' in The Examiner (1710), and the 'boots' form — 'A lie will go round the world while truth is pulling its boots on' — circulated in the 19th century, commonly credited to the preacher C. H. Spurgeon, who himself presented it as an old saying. 'Pants on' is a 20th-century Americanized rewrite. Versions of this line are also misattributed to Mark Twain, another magnet. There is no evidence Churchill originated it.
suggested_reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century

earliest_print_source: The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, Sogyal Rinpoche, 1992
notes: The two-selves passage — the garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating ego versus the hidden spiritual being whose still voice of wisdom is rarely heard — is characteristic of and, to my knowledge, drawn from 'The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying' (1992). I am confident about the book but not about chapter or page, and the corpus text appears spliced: the closing clause ('you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide') does not grammatically follow the preceding sentence and looks like material lifted from further down the same passage. Recommend re-checking against the book and repairing the ellipsis before promotion.

I know of nothing in Kierkegaard's authorship resembling this, in any standard translation. The diction is modern therapeutic/mindfulness aphorism — the Gestalt 'paradoxical theory of change' register — not Kierkegaard's, whose treatment of becoming is far more elaborated and anguished. It reads like a coaching-literature line that acquired a prestigious name. I cannot identify the real originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but I would not promote this under Kierkegaard's name.

Genuine Kierkegaard, from the 'Diapsalmata' aphorisms opening Either/Or Part I (1843), written in the voice of the aesthete 'A'. Familiar in both the Swenson and Hong translations. The original aphorism continues '...For pleasure disappoints, possibility never' — the corpus text truncates before that clause, which is a legitimate excerpt rather than a distortion. Note for the record that the speaker is a pseudonymous persona, as with most of Kierkegaard's aesthetic writing.

This is the opening of the well-known passage on money in Sri Aurobindo's short book 'The Mother' (1928), in the section treating money as one of the powers to be conquered and returned to the Divine. The wording matches the standard Sri Aurobindo Ashram edition as I know it. Confident in book and passage; slightly short of 0.9 only because I cannot confirm the section numbering.

Self-transcendence and 'competing only with yourself' were central, endlessly repeated themes of Sri Chinmoy's talks and writings, and the vocabulary here is authentically his. But he published hundreds of volumes of aphorisms and transcribed lectures, and I cannot locate this specific text in any of them; the ellipsis suggests it has been assembled from more than one sentence. Attribution is plausible and stylistically consistent, but uncited.

Anachronistic. 'Unconditional self acceptance' is a term of art from Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and the whole passage — separating mistakes from intrinsic worth, 'a peaceful mind' — is 20th-century cognitive-therapy and self-esteem language with no counterpart in the devotional writing of a 17th-century bishop. Francis de Sales wrote about gentleness toward one's own faults, which is probably why his name attached itself here, but his framing is theological (worth grounded in God), not psychological. I cannot identify who actually wrote this, so I am proposing no reattribution; Ellis is the likely conceptual source rather than a confirmed author.

This one is genuinely at home in Francis de Sales: gentleness in the face of difficulty, and the counsel to bend rather than break, are signatures of his spiritual direction in 'Introduction to the Devout Life' and his letters. It appears in Catholic devotional compilations of his sayings, usually paired with 'Do not lose your inner peace for anything whatsoever.' I cannot pin it to a specific letter or chapter, and translation-era English makes exact matching hard, so no citation. Moderate confidence, unlike q_1292 which I judge to be a modern fabrication under the same name.

This belongs to the same apocryphal cluster as 'Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words' — a line Franciscan scholars have repeatedly shown is absent from Francis's writings and from the early biographies. The 'walking is our preaching' version derives from a later retelling of an anecdote about Francis walking through town with a companion, and appears in modern devotional literature rather than in any source contemporary with him. Not found in the Writings of Francis or in Celano/Bonaventure as far as I know.

No evidence connects this to Francis of Assisi. It does not appear in his authenticated writings or in the early Franciscan biographies, and the earliest instances I am aware of are 20th-century, in motivational and recovery literature, where it circulated for some time before Francis's name was attached. The rhetorical shape — necessary, possible, impossible — is a modern three-beat inspirational construction. Widely repeated, which is not evidence.

Stanley Horowitz is a real and otherwise obscure figure best known for a Reader's Digest contest-winning line about the seasons ('Winter is an etching, spring a watercolor...'). This aphorism is consistently credited to him in quotation collections, which suggests a shared original source — plausibly the same magazine-filler context — but I cannot identify a publication or date. Attribution is stable but entirely uncited.

Consistent with Covey's Habit 1 material on proactivity and the freedom to choose one's response, which he built explicitly on Viktor Frankl. The sentiment is authentically his and the attribution is stable, but I cannot place this exact sentence in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) or 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991), and Covey also said versions of this in many talks. Note the underlying idea traces to Frankl, not Covey.

Stephen Larsen is a real author — Joseph Campbell's biographer, with Robin Larsen, of 'A Fire in the Mind' — and this passage is written in a Campbellian register, which is precisely the problem: 'say yes to life even though you know it will devour you' echoes Campbell's affirmation-of-life and 'joyful participation in the sorrows of the world' themes closely enough that the two men's names could easily have been swapped in transmission. I cannot place the text in Larsen's own books, nor confirm it as a Campbell quotation. Uncertain enough that I am proposing no reattribution.

Authentically Levine in vocabulary and cadence — 'letting go', meeting oneself anew, healing as distinct from curing are the core of his work with the dying. Most likely from 'Healing into Life and Death' (1987) or 'Who Dies?' (1982), but I cannot confirm which, so no citation. Attribution stable across sources and stylistically sound; uncited.

Same assessment as q_1299: the framing — that becoming loving is subtractive, a letting go of accreted self-concept rather than an achievement — is a recognizable Stephen Levine teaching, and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I cannot identify the book. Uncited, and the opening sentence's grammar ('People ask what must they become') suggests transcription from a talk rather than from print.

The four human endowments — self-awareness, conscience, independent will, creative imagination — are a genuine and distinctive Covey framework, presented in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) and developed further in 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991). Attribution to Covey is not in doubt. The circulating text, with its ellipsis, is a condensation rather than a verbatim sentence from either book, which is why I am not citing a page or crossing the promotion bar. Note this is the same author as q_1297, entered under a different name form ('Stephen Covey' vs 'Stephen R. Covey') — worth normalizing in the corpus.

Sounds like Covey speaking rather than writing — the direct second-person challenge and the appeal to 'universal principles' are his, but the loose, spoken syntax points to a seminar or interview rather than a book. I cannot place it in any of his published works. Plausible, uncited.

Steve DeMasco is a real figure — Shaolin martial artist and author of 'The Shaolin Way' (2006) — and this line is consistently credited to him, plausibly from that book or from an interview around its publication. I cannot confirm the source. The quote is generic enough that stable attribution carries little evidential weight on its own.
